newsitem.title: USA: Intl Paper Box board is ousted.
newsitem.headline: Intl Paper Box board is ousted.

text.p: The board of directors of International Paper Box Machine Co was ousted on Saturday by dissident shareholders seeking to sell the 93-year-old privately held company, a lawyer for the dissidents said.
International Paper Box makes machines that cut, fold and glue cereal boxes and orange juice cartons. The Nashua-based firm's sales average $20 million annually.
The ouster of the board clears the way for a sale of the family-owned business to J&L Co of Louisiana, said the lawyer, Edward Hahn.

"The group of shareholders that brought this action believe they should seriously consider the sale of the company and that ... it is in the best interest of the shareholders," Hahn said in an interview at his Manchester office shortly after the Saturday shareholder meeting at which the board was ousted.
Company officials had rejected the dissidents' proposal to sell the company for a reported $8 million.
Company President Louis Chagnon had sought a $4.8 million loan from Fleet Bank-New Hampshire to buy out the dissidents, which included Hugh McAdams, a former vice president-sales.
Chagnon convinced New Hampshire's Business Finance Authority to provide a loan guarantee to help stop a "hostile takeover."

Dissident shareholders disputed Chagnon's claim. "This is not a hostile takeover...the proposal was open, it was publicized, it required the apporval of the company's board of directors and the company's shareholders. That's not a hostile takeover," Hahn said.

The decision by the state to issue a loan guarantee was unprecedented, state officials said. While guarantees have been granted to help companies relocate, buy equipment or pay for sewage treatment facilties, guarantees had never been issued to stop a merger or acquisition, they said.
"Obviously, our interest is in retaining local ownership. International Paper Box employs aobut 150 people. Our interest is in retaining employment there," said Jack Donovan, BFA executive director.
Hahn maintains that no evidence has surfaced that the potential new owner of the company intends to liquidate assets or lay off employees.
The new board of directors is expected to begin deliberations leading to the sale of the firm.
